drills.q: Trace the exact output order: console.log(1); setTimeout(()=>console.log(2),0); Promise.resolve().then(()=>console.log(3)); console.log(4);
drills.a: 1, 4, 3, 2. Synchronous code runs to completion first (1, 4). The microtask queue then drains fully before any macrotask runs (3). Only then does the setTimeout macrotask run (2).

drills.q: Define microtask vs macrotask and give two examples of each, plus the ordering rule between them.
drills.a: Macrotasks (setTimeout/setInterval, UI events, I/O callbacks) -- only one runs per event loop iteration. Microtasks (Promise .then/.catch/.finally, queueMicrotask) -- the ENTIRE queue drains, including newly-added ones, before the next macrotask or paint.

drills.q: Why does a for(var i...) loop with setTimeout inside log the same final value 3 times, but for(let j...) logs 0,1,2?
drills.a: var is function-scoped -- one shared binding across all iterations, so by the time any callback fires (after the sync loop completes), the variable holds its final value. let creates a fresh binding per iteration by specification, so each closure captures its own distinct value.

drills.q: State the four this-binding rules in precedence order and explain why arrow functions are the exception.
drills.a: new binding > explicit (call/apply/bind) > implicit (obj.method(), determined by call site) > default (undefined in strict mode / global otherwise). Arrow functions have no own this slot at all -- they lexically capture this from their enclosing scope at definition time and cannot be rebound by any of the four rules.

drills.q: Explain the prototype chain and how class/extends relates to it mechanically.
drills.a: Every object has an internal [[Prototype]] link; property lookup checks own properties then walks the chain until it finds a match or hits null. class/extends is syntax sugar that sets up exactly this chain automatically (Dog.prototype.__proto__ = Animal.prototype) -- not a separate inheritance mechanism. instanceof walks this same chain looking for the constructor's .prototype, it isn't a stored type tag.

drills.q: Contrast ES modules and CommonJS on resolution, binding semantics, and loading -- not just syntax.
drills.a: ESM: static resolution (analyzable before execution), LIVE read-only bindings (an import reflects later updates in the source module), async by spec, supports top-level await. CommonJS: dynamic require() (a real function call, can be conditional), VALUE COPY at require-time (later reassignment in the source isn't seen), synchronous loading.

drills.q: What is a dual-package hazard and why is it still a real problem in 2026?
drills.a: When a package is instantiated twice in the same dependency tree -- once via require() and once via import -- producing two separate module instances whose instanceof checks and any shared module-level state diverge. It remains real because the npm ecosystem has decades of CJS-only packages and ESM/CJS interop is not a fully solved problem at the tooling level.

drills.q: What does `await` actually desugar to, and trace: async function f(){ console.log('a'); await null; console.log('b'); } console.log('start'); f(); console.log('end');
drills.a: await expr is equivalent to Promise.resolve(expr).then(continuation) -- everything after await runs as a microtask. f() runs synchronously to the first await ('a'), then returns control to the caller. Output: start, a, end, b.

drills.q: Two independent async operations are called with `await a(); await b();`. What's wrong and what's the fix?
drills.a: Sequential await forces b() to not even start until a() fully resolves, serializing independent work (total latency ~= a+b instead of max(a,b)). Fix: start both first (const pa = a(), pb = b();) then await Promise.all([pa, pb]).

drills.q: A recursive .then() chain with no terminating condition freezes a page that is still visibly using CPU. Explain the mechanism and how to fix it.
drills.a: The microtask queue must fully drain -- including new microtasks enqueued during the drain -- before the loop can proceed to the next macrotask or repaint. A chain that keeps scheduling a new microtask from within its own .then() never lets the drain finish, starving rendering and pending macrotasks indefinitely. Fix: insert an actual macrotask boundary periodically, e.g. setTimeout(next, 0) instead of Promise.resolve().then(next).

drills.q: Explain why a generator's local variables persist across .next() calls, and how this differs from a closure-based counter object.
drills.a: A generator's execution context (including local variables and its position in the function body) is suspended, not discarded, between .next() calls -- each resumes exactly where the last yield paused. Unlike a closure-based counter (which only exposes whatever methods you explicitly write), a generator natively implements the iterator protocol and can be consumed directly by for...of, spread, and destructuring, and can pause mid-expression or mid-loop anywhere a yield appears.

drills.q: Why does `this` log undefined when a regular (non-arrow) object method is passed directly as `element.addEventListener('click', obj.method)`?
drills.a: this is determined by the call site, not the definition site. Passing obj.method by reference detaches it from obj -- when the browser invokes the bare function reference (or binds this to the DOM element itself, per addEventListener's own behavior), the original obj context is lost. Fix: pass an arrow function wrapper or .bind(obj) the method before passing it.

drills.q: Distinguish Promise.all and Promise.allSettled behavior on partial failure, and when you'd choose each.
drills.a: Promise.all rejects immediately with the first rejection reason without waiting for the others to settle (though they continue running in the background, their outcomes are lost to the caller). Promise.allSettled waits for every promise to settle regardless of individual failures and returns a status/value or status/reason for each. Choose allSettled when you need to know the outcome of all operations even if some fail; Promise.all when any single failure should short-circuit the whole operation.
